# Debate: Four-day work week

- Mode: debate
- Cast: Amara Okafor (prop), Victor Hale (prop), Mei Tanaka-Ruiz (opp)
- Motion: This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week.

**—**: ROUND 1 · OPENING

**Amara Okafor** [neutral]: I'll take the clinical angle, because that's what I know. Our own review followed 1,140 clinical staff and found fatigue is rising and measurable, with the length of consecutive shift blocks, not just total hours, as the strongest predictor of how exhausted people feel [^1]. Two wards that piloted a four-day compressed rota saw burnout fall by roughly a fifth in twelve weeks, sleep before shifts improve by around 40 minutes, and patient throughput, length of stay and readmissions all stay within normal variation [^2][^1]. So my first reason: a four-day week with protected rest days is a health and safety intervention, and we have local evidence it works without costing patient care. My second: burnout in our emergency department climbed from 29% to 41% over the year, and voluntary nursing resignations hit 14%, each replacement costing about four months of salary [^1] — that is a workforce sustainability argument, not a perk. And my third: the pilot staff named the guaranteed rest days, not the longer shifts, as the change that mattered most [^2], which tells me the design detail is what we should be arguing about, and the motion gets that design right in principle. Let's figure out what's actually going on before we decide this can't be done.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [neutral]: Opposition, then. Three reasons, and yes, they're hedged, because anyone who gives you one number on this is selling something. First, the pilots everyone cites aren't a mandate. The summaries themselves recommend sector-specific trials in health, transport and care with independent measurement before any national standard [^3], and those are precisely the sectors where coverage can't be turned off on a Friday. Second, the gains came from redesign, not from the calendar. Firms that halved meetings and reworked workflows got results; firms that just deleted a day squeezed five into four, longer days, weekend email, and roughly half the burnout improvement [^4]. That's a management intervention wearing a four-day costume, and you can't legislate workflow redesign across an economy. Third, and this is the second-order bit nobody prices, a nationwide standard hits small firms and shift-based services hardest, so the distributional answer swamps the average. Adopt it and you've chosen a headline over a mechanism.

**Victor Hale** [neutral]: Kai, Mei — allow me to fix the terms before anyone fixes the conclusion. Nationwide means a default standard week in law, not an identical timetable for every employer; adopt means legislate a transition, not flip a switch on Monday. Three reasons. First, the status quo is also a policy, and it must justify itself: exhaustion is already billed to us as sickness absence, agency fees and resignations, and I will be asking the other side for their figure on that[^5]. Second, this is not novel machinery — the 1931 Act made the two-day weekend default and still gave agriculture and shipping a ten-year transition [^5], and continuous-coverage sectors already run on shift rules under Part IV of the Code. Third, phases work: sector trials, collective agreements first, the public sector as model employer. Amara has given you the evidence; I give you the timetable.

**—**: ROUND 2 · REBUTTAL

**MODERATOR**: Concrete numbers this round, please. Everyone.

**MODERATOR**: Mei, give us a number. What does this cost?

**Victor Hale** [neutral]: Numbers, then, and I'll name the strongest point against us first: Mei's distributional objection — a nationwide default hits small firms and shift-based services hardest, so the average hides the harm. That is the sharpest thing said in this room, and it deserves a real answer, not a wave. So: her own cited summaries recommend sector trials and independent measurement before a national standard; I accept that, and I say a transition schedule *is* the national standard — a floor with a phase-in is not a headline, it's a mechanism. Now my numbers. Burnout in that emergency department rose 29% to 41% in a year; voluntary nursing resignations hit 14%; each replacement costs roughly four months of salary. Multiply 14% by a workforce of, say, 1,000 nurses and you are funding 140 replacements a year at four months' salary each — that is not a perk, it is a leak. The compressed rota cut burnout by about a fifth in twelve weeks, sleep improved around 40 minutes, and throughput, length of stay and readmissions stayed inside normal variation. Small firms get the phase-in and the public-sector model; the leak gets fixed. Urgent, not novel.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: A number, then, with the honest error bars attached. In the nine shift-based organisations that tried this, holding coverage constant took between 18% and 27% more staffed hours, met through new hires, overtime or agency cover [^6]. That's the cost, and it lands precisely where Victor's phase-in can't reach: nights, weekends, the emergency department, the care home. On his own arithmetic, 140 replacements a year — you can fund a lot of that leak without a statutory calendar. Two of the nine recovered part of that cost through lower sickness and turnover; the other seven didn't measure it [^6], which tells you the payback is plausible, not established. And note where the savings came from: managers redrawing rotas, not the day off itself. So the national default hands the extra-hours bill to every small shift-based employer while the productivity dividend stays optional and unmeasured. Urgent, maybe. Affordable at scale, no.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: Strongest point on the other side, and I'll say it plainly: the leak is real. Exhaustion already gets billed to us as sickness absence, agency fees and resignations, so the status quo isn't free and nobody should pretend it is. But that's a case for fixing the leak, not for a nationwide four-day default, because the evidence doesn't tell us the calendar is the fix. Two wards with a compressed rota cut burnout by roughly a fifth while throughput held — grant it entirely. That was one hospital, twelve weeks, with managers actively rebuilding the rota. My nine-organisation figure is the other half of the same story: where coverage had to be held constant, staffed hours rose 18% to 27%, and only two of the nine even measured the turnover savings that would pay it back. So the honest reading is: design works, and design doesn't scale by mandate. On my own case — a nationwide standard binds the employers with the least slack first, small care homes, night pharmacies, rural clinics, the exact places already running thin. A floor with a phase-in is still a floor, and floors don't care whether you can staff them. So the cost isn't the headline; it's the incidence, and the incidence is regressive. Fund the redesign sector by sector, publish the numbers, and revisit.

**Amara Okafor** [thinking]: Victor has covered the mechanism, so I'll take the strongest thing Mei said: that holding coverage constant cost 18 to 27 percent more staffed hours, and that the bill lands on the smallest, thinnest employers first. That's a serious finding and I won't wave it away. But look at what it actually measured: overtime and agency cover used to fill a schedule that hadn't been redesigned. That 18 to 27 percent price tag is the cost of doing this badly, and we already know from our own rota work that the redesign is the part that saves you money. You don't fund the fix by protecting the leak. Second, and this is the part nobody prices: every Monday an exhausted nurse calls in sick, that shift still gets covered — by agency, at a premium, with a stranger who doesn't know the ward. The status quo is also paying the 18 to 27 percent, just without a design attached. Mei's own two-of-nine figure shows the payback is plausible; the honest move is to phase in, measure, and publish, which is exactly what a statutory floor with a transition lets you do. Urgent, yes. Novel, no. Affordable at scale — that's the question the phase-in answers, not dodges.

**—**: ROUND 3 · CLOSING

**Amara Okafor** [thinking]: Two things were left open, and I'll name them honestly. First, whether a national default forces hours up or lets them stay flat — Mei's nine organisations say up when coverage isn't redesigned, our two wards say flat when it is. Second, whether the turnover savings actually pay for it, which only two of those nine bothered to measure. Neither side has closed that gap tonight, and I won't pretend otherwise.

But here's why we still win. The motion asks whether we'd adopt a standard, and a standard is the only thing that makes those open questions answerable at scale. Right now the leak is real, unmeasured, and paid by the people least able to absorb it — the nurse on her third consecutive Monday, the care home running thin. Adopting a floor with a phase-in doesn't claim the dividend is proven. It sets up the trial that proves it, sector by sector, and it stops pretending the current schedule is free. Design works; a mandate is how we find out if design scales. On tonight's evidence, that's the stronger case.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: What's still open is the thing that decides this: whether a statutory floor forces staffed hours up or leaves them flat, and whether the turnover savings ever repay the cost. Amara is right that neither side closed it tonight, and I won't pretend my nine organisations settled it — two of nine measured the payback, seven didn't, error bars wide enough to drive a rota through. On that half-open question, the stronger case isn't the one that legislates a default and runs the trial afterwards; it's the one that runs the trial and legislates if it holds. You can fund sector redesign, publish the numbers, and revisit — that's a mechanism too, and it doesn't hand the 18-to-27% extra-hours bill to the smallest, thinnest employers in the meantime. Design works. Whether design scales is exactly what we don't know yet, and adopting a nationwide floor is the one move that makes learning it harder, because you've already committed the money before the measurement. The status quo isn't free; I've said so. But an unknown floor isn't either, and "urgency" isn't evidence that the calendar is the fix. On tonight's record, Opposition.

**Victor Hale** [thinking]: Amara has drawn the line correctly, so I will only stand on it. What remains open is a question of arithmetic, not verdict: does a redesigned rota hold staffed hours flat, and does turnover savings repay the cost. I concede we did not close it tonight. But notice whose burden that open question actually serves. Every measurement Mei wants — which sectors pay more, which recoup — can only be gathered where a standard requires the numbers to be gathered. Right now nobody counts the leak, which is precisely why it survives. Define the terms, and the count begins. A floor with a phase-in is not a commitment to the money before the measurement; it is the measurement, written into law with a timetable attached. The 1931 weekend faced the same objection and answered it with a ten-year transition. I ask you to adopt the motion, for the nurse on her third Monday, and for the evidence we cannot presently see.

**—**: ROUND 4 · VERDICT

**—**: STRONGER CASE: OPPOSITION

## Verdict

Stronger case: opp

The Opposition scored higher on evidence, rebuttal, clarity and persuasion, and its case turned the debate onto the open question of extra staffed hours and unmeasured payback. The Proposition conceded that gap and asked the motion to be judged as the trial that answers it, which left the Opposition's trial-first alternative standing as the stronger case.

## Sources

[^1]: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025, p. 1. "- Staff who slept under six hours before a shift were twice as likely to report a near-miss medication error that week. - Two wards that piloted a compressed rota saw burnout fall by roughly a fifth in twelve weeks, with no loss of patient throughput. - Voluntary nursing resignations reached 14% over the year, and each replacement costs about four months of salary."
[^2]: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025, p. 7. "## 6. The compressed-rota pilot Two wards piloted a compressed rota: four longer days, then three days off."
[^3]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 8. "## 7. Recommendations The authors recommend sector-specific trials in health, transport and care, with independent measurement of output and service quality, before any national standard is set."
[^4]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 4. "Common redesign steps included: - cutting standing meetings to 25 minutes, or replacing them with written updates; - "focus blocks" of two to three hours with no messages; - clearing duplicated approval steps; - agreeing in advance how to cover customers on the day off. Firms that skipped redesign often saw workers squeeze five days of work into four, with longer days and weekend email."
[^5]: Moot court notes, ¶ 2. "¶ 6. Closing options: res ipsa loquitur; "the destination is agreed". Don't sound triumphant. Judges reward conceding a fair point gracefully. ¶ 7. Definitions first. "Nationwide" means the default standard week in law, not an identical schedule for every employer. "Adopt" means legislate a standard with a transition, not switch overnight."
[^6]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 6. "The nine were three private clinics, two call centres, two security firms, a hotel group and a logistics depot. In each, managers redesigned rotas rather than hours, and the cost came from covering the hours that productivity gains could not replace."
